sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Hocking County
sections.html:
Hocking County deeds go to the ground-level office inside the courthouse at 1 East Main Street, Logan. Mail goes to P.O. Box 949, Logan, OH 43138. Call 740-385-2031 for the office or 740-385-0377 for fax.

Two clocks apply. Visitors are welcome until 4 in the afternoon, but recording stops at half past three, the same cutoff as copy requests, and the research room shuts at 3:45. In bad weather the office opens at 10 a.m. under a Level 2 snow advisory and stays closed under Level 3, so phone before driving in from the Hocking Hills side.

The index covers records from 1818, and electronic indexing began on January 1, 1992. Buchtel, Laurelville and Murray City use the same counter as everyone else in the county. The office also links an online payment portal and a land records search from its page.

The county posts its own fee sheet. Recording costs a flat $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after, and that price includes a $5 restoration fee. Payment can be made at the counter.

Hocking County Recorder fees
ServiceCharge
Recording, first two pages$39
Recording, each page after$8
Marginal reference$4 each
Document that breaks the layout rules$20
Print made in the office$1 a page
Print made by staff, or an emailed copy$2 a page

The office does not run title searches, give legal advice or prepare documents. Have the deed drafted ahead of time by your closing agent or lawyer, then bring it in with the payment.

House Bill 525 created the layout standards, now section 317.114 of the Revised Code, effective July 1, 2009. A deed that falls short costs $20 more. Hocking's counter checks each deed against this list:

  • Print no smaller than 10 point, in black or blue ink. Highlighter is never allowed.
  • Leave a one inch border down both sides and along the foot of every sheet.
  • Keep the top three inches of page one blank for the recorder, auditor and engineer stamps. Later pages need only an inch and a half.

Court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD-214 discharges, state or federal documents and anything signed before the law took effect are exempt. A deed you draft yourself is not. If you are selling without an agent, check the margins before you print the signature page.

The county's list is long, and a seller's file may touch several items on it. Deeds can be warranty, quit claim, survivorship or sheriff's deeds. Mortgage papers include releases, assumptions, assignments, subordinations and waivers of priority. The office also files certificates of transfer, affidavits, easements, leases, land contracts, plats, condominium records, powers of attorney and trusts.

A title search will turn up liens, so read this part of the county's list closely:

  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement.
  • Federal tax liens and personal tax liens.
  • Workers' compensation and unemployment compensation liens.
  • Child support liens and Medicaid fraud liens.

If you know of one, tell your buyer or title company early. Annexations, street name changes and vacated streets and alleys are also recorded here, which can affect a rural lot's frontage.

sections.h2: The auditor and the conveyance fee
sections.html:
The auditor sees the deed first and collects the Ohio conveyance fee. Call 740-385-2127 for the figure on your sale price. The auditor's tools menu includes a calculator that adds a parcel transfer fee to its answer. Ask at the same time whether the county levies a real property transfer tax, since that is optional for each county.

A January 2026 message on the auditor's site says short-term rentals are now valued apart from residential property, at their market value as short-term rentals. If you are selling a cabin near the state park, ask how the parcel is classified before you quote taxes to a buyer.

The same message says the budget commission, commissioners and township trustees trimmed inside millage so collections stayed near the 2024 level after the 2025 valuation update. Without that, the auditor estimates inside millage would have drawn about $1.25 million more, a 22% increase.

sections.h2: Reducing or contesting a tax bill
sections.html:
The owner occupancy credit, once called the 2 1/2% reduction, is for owners who live in the house as their main residence. File with the auditor between January 1 and the first Monday in June. It does not cover rentals, corporate or partnership owners, units in commercial buildings, taxed manufactured homes and acreage beyond one acre.

If you disagree with the value, the Board of Revision hears appeals filed with the auditor from January 1 through March 31. The board is made up of the treasurer, the auditor and the president of the commissioners. The best evidence is a recent sale price shown by closing papers, or sales of comparable homes, plus photographs of the property's condition.

A late-payment penalty can be removed on request for these reasons:

  • You never got a correct bill and made an effort to get one.
  • Your payment was mailed on time with a proper postmark but never processed.
  • Serious injury, death or a hospital stay within 60 days before the due date, with payment inside 60 days after it.
  • A mistake made by the auditor or treasurer.
  • Reasonable cause without willful neglect, for owners timely in each of the last three years.

The treasurer is in Suite 201 of the courthouse, phone 740-385-3517. If you sell near a collection date, ask the treasurer to confirm that both halves of the year's bill have posted before closing.

Five state tax bills were signed December 19, 2025. House Bill 186 raises the owner occupancy credit from 2.5% toward 15.38% by tax year 2029 and phases out the 10% non-business credit, and House Bill 335 slows growth in inside millage to the rate of inflation. Most of that shows up on bills from 2027 on.

The county also runs a land bank. It acquires vacant, abandoned and tax-foreclosed properties, waives delinquent taxes on property it takes, and deed-restricts residential parcels to prevent nightly rentals. Owners of worthless or low-value parcels can offer them to the bank instead of leaving them to a tax foreclosure. Houses the bank sells go to buyers who show a need for single-family housing and agree to owner-occupy.

sections.h2: Housing numbers that help set a price
sections.html: Hocking County had 27,512 people in July 2025 and 13,024 housing units. Owners live in 78.8% of occupied homes, the typical home value is $186,400, typical rent is $808 and household income is about $62,960. Lodging and restaurant sales were high for the region, which points to a visitor economy. A seller near the park should not assume every buyer wants a year-round home.

sections.h2: A typical sequence for a sale
sections.html: Most Hocking County sales follow the same path. Your closing agent or lawyer drafts the deed to the layout rules above. You sign it, and the auditor collects the conveyance fee. The deed then goes to the recorder before 3:30 p.m., with the recording charge. Any mortgage release your lender files after payoff is recorded at the same counter, so ask your title company to confirm both were filed.

faqs.q: How much is a Hocking County recording?
faqs.a: A flat $39 covers the first two pages, and each extra page adds $8, including a $5 restoration fee. A deed that breaks the layout rules adds $20.

faqs.q: When does the Hocking County Recorder stop taking documents?
faqs.a: At 3:30 p.m. on weekdays. The office stays open to visitors until 4:00, and the research room closes at 3:45.

faqs.q: Can I order a copy of a recorded deed by email?
faqs.a: Yes. Emailed copies cost $2 per page, and requests should arrive by 3:30 p.m. A copy printed at the office costs $1 per page.

faqs.q: Who collects the Ohio conveyance fee in Hocking County?
faqs.a: The county auditor. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the larger of $1 or ten cents per $100 of value, and the auditor's calculator shows the figure with a parcel transfer fee.

faqs.q: Will the recorder write my deed or check my title?
faqs.a: No. The office cannot perform title searches, give legal advice or prepare documents, so leave those steps to a closing agent or attorney.
